[1] "load /home/skhan/data/soybeandata/5x/data_files/gmax_bed.bed"
Error in unique(splitn(genes.obj$id, "_", 3)) :
  error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for function 'unique': Error in FUN(X[[1L]], ...) : subscript out of bounds

How can I make this bed file work. If not what should I do to generate a bed file that works with eDMR.

I tried contacting the author of eDMR software but she is not responding.

Kindly suggest me what needs to be done. I really need these results desperately.

regards

ah got it!, treatment vector should have 1s and 0s only when going into the calculateDiffMeth() function. it can have multiple values for other functions for clustering for example but since we are only testing case vs control it should have this format. You can search the discussion group if it is not clear what is compared against what, somebody asked that question recently.

setting treatment= c(1,1,1,0,0,0) should work in your first example.

I also have another question about methylkit: In the current work flow, we can "tileMethylCounts" and then "unite" samples to get the common sliding windows, but this sometimes causes problems (e.g., in a 100-bp window, it is possible that in some samples only 1 CpG is detected, but in other samples 10 CpGs are detected; comparison in this case might lead to obvious false-positive hits). I wondered if we could take the common CpGs (unite the samples) first and then "tileMethylCounts" the the common CpGs?

Best,
Li

messages.subject: "cov.bases" in "tileMethylCounts"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Altuna,

I have a question regarding the "tileMethylCounts" function: According to the methylkit document, "cov.bases" is the minimum number of bases to be covered in a given window, and the default value is 0. When the value is 0, my understanding is that a window is generated even when it does not contain any sampled CpG, and thus the number of windows for each sample should be the same (as the number of windows in this case is only affected by the genome size). However, the actual numbers of windows generated in each samples are still slightly different when cov.bases=0. So I wondered what exactly does "cov.bases" mean? Does "cov.bases=0" require at least 1 sampled CpG in the window?

Thank you very much!

Best,
Li

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] "cov.bases" in "tileMethylCounts"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Li,
If there is no CpG covered in the window, a window will not be generated, but number of covered bases should be greater than or equal to "cov.bases". The default could have been 1 as well but it doesn't change anything, since there should be at least 1 CpG covered to create the window. Technically the window is created by discarded later on if it doesn't overlap with a covered base. Only after then cov.bases threshold is applied.

covered >= cov.bases

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] error when using Benjamini-Hochberg procedure in "calculateDiffMeth"
messages.subject_clean: [methylkit_discussion] error when using Benjamini-Hochberg procedure in "calculateDiffMeth"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Li,
that's how usually a logistic regression model (binomial GLM) is fit to proportional data. You need those weights to be able to calculate some statistics in the model correctly and to correct for the observations that have low sample size (meaning coverage, similar to number of trials in binomial distribution ). More coverage means more information and these points should have larger effect than points with small coverage. I think it would be unconventional, even incorrect to remove weights from binomial GLM where the response is a proportion.  If you are not interested in coverage and the value it brings to the model, just use a t-test.

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: Methylkit usage for 'unite'
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using methylkit for RRBS data. I have 19 samples as test/treatment_0 and 15 samples as control/treatment_1. I want to perform 'unite' function on these samples. However, the way i want to use this function is different from the way it works.

I want to apply the unite function on equal percentage of samples. For example, I want CpGs which are represented in 80% of the samples (=15 in test samples and 10 in control, numbers were rounded off). However, to my understanding methylkit only allows 'unite' command to function in terms of numbers equally applicable on both treatment conditions ie., I have only option to choose  a definite number of samples which contain a particular CpG (ie., I have to choose min.pergroup=14L and this implies 73% samples in test condition and 93% in control)

Is there a way where I can choose to run 'unite' function to be applicable on equal percentage of samples(ie., min.pergroup = 80 which means 15 samples in test and 10 samples in control) ? In the other case can I choose to apply 'unite' function with separate 'min.pergroup' selection on each treatment (ie., min.pergroup.treatment0=15 and min.pergroup.treatment1=10).

Regards,
Kalyan

Here are couple of alternatives how to achieve your goal:

1)You can check out the code in github, add this functionality and make a pull request or just use it for your own purpose.

2)Alternatively, you can just write a new unite() function let's call it unite2() that implements this functionality as an R function that is not part of the package. Example of such a function is here (just an example, it is not doing what you need to do):
https://gist.github.com/al2na/a9ea925fc11af26b9c72

3) use the unite function in the package with min.per.group=10L, then filter the methylBase object on the test group of samples so that the test group has at least 15 samples covered for a given CpG.

Best,
Altuna

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using methylKitR for the analysis of differentially methylated regions. Please let me know
i) how can I mention/incorporate in-house assembly in this command: (For hg18 and mm9, it is automatically considered)
myobj=read( file.list,
           sample.id=list("test1","test2","ctrl1","ctrl2"),assembly="hg18",treatment=c(1,1,0,0))

ii) Regarding annotation of DMR, can following command works with a bed file containing only 4 columns (Chromosome name, Start, End, Score) instead of all the 10 columns. Will it affect the subsequent annotation steps?

gene.obj=read.transcript.features(system.file("extdata", "refseq.hg18.bed.txt",
+ package = "methylKit"))

Please reply.

Shalu Jhanwar
PhD student
Barcelona, Spain

> myobj=read( file.list,
>            sample.id=list("test1","test2","ctrl1","ctrl2"),assembly="hg18",treatment=c(1,1,0,0))

That's just a string for the information of the user,  you can put whatever at the moment. Just make sure samples from the same assembly have the same string.

>
> ii) Regarding annotation of DMR, can following command works with a bed file containing only 4 columns (Chromosome name, Start, End, Score) instead of all the 10 columns. Will it affect the subsequent annotation steps?
>
> gene.obj=read.transcript.features(system.file("extdata", "refseq.hg18.bed.txt",
> + package = "methylKit"))
>

> I guess you want to use read.bed() then annotate.WithFeature() in this case.  read.transcript.features() is for reading bed12 files that have exon/intron structure.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kalyan,
I think easiest for you will be option 3. Where you use unite() with min.per.group=10L, then filter the returning object to make sure test group has at least 15 samples covered.

assume obj is the methylBase object. Below is an example of how to achieve this, I haven't tested the code but something along these lines will work.

data=getData(obj)

# this piece gets a TRUE/FALSE data.frame for the test samples
# where TRUE indicates that sample has coverage
filter=!is.na <http://is.na>( data[  o...@coverage.index[obj@treatment==0]  ])

# filter based on the number of samples in the test group that have
# at least 15 samples covered
new.obj=obj[rowSums(filter)>=15,]

but for reference unite function is here:
https://github.com/al2na/methylKit/blob/development/R/backbone.R#L535

> i) Following my previous question, is there no use of assembly, it is merely a string that needs to provide for user's information?

This is for the user and some of the functions, for example the package will not let you merge methylRaw objects if they have different assembly strings.

> ii) Regarding annotation, there is no annotation information is given in the refseq.hg18.bed.txt in any column. Then how is methylKitR able to decide the annotation boundaries (e.g. exons, introns, promoters etc) on the basis of co-ordinates. Does it take assembly into consideration at this step?
>

Read about the BED format description. BED12 format has that information. As a user you have to make sure you use the CpG methylation information from the same assembly as the BED file. Most bed files will not have an assembly information embedded in the file, that's why we can't check if the annotation assembly and methylKit object assembly matches or not.

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] reported differentially methylated promoter regions does not contain differentially methylated bases
messages.subject_clean: [methylkit_discussion] reported differentially methylated promoter regions does not contain differentially methylated bases
messages.body_plain:
I wouldn't expect the differentially methylated bases on promoters will be always overlapping with differentially methylated promoters from the regional analysis. One is looking at the bases, the other at regions and when you sum up the methylated and unmethylated bases overlapping with a region you change the statistics, it can go either way, it can push the region to be differentially methylated although individual bases are not DMCs in your thresholds. You see most of your differentially methylated promoters are borderline close to 25% threshold.

The proper way to check and report this it is to find all promoter overlapping DMCs and then check what percent of those promoters overlapping with DMCs are differentially methylated promoters from your promoterMeth.r script. If they never overlap there might be a problem.

Best,
Altuna

messages.body_plain:
in any case, I think you don't have enough memory for the task at hand. It takes time and memory to read large files.

1. Filter the CpGs that have coverage below 10X from the files
2. if 1 is not enough, you should be able to split the files based on their chromosome, it is an  awk one liner. see here:http://seqanswers.com/forums/showthread.php?t=8115

then, in a for loop, read the files for each chromosome and use unite() to merge them into one table per chromosome, append each methylBase object to a result list.
After you exit the loop you can try to merge the data in the list. I can help you in more detail if you can get to that stage. But try the first suggestion.

best,
Altuna

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] warnings from calculateDiffMeth function
messages.body_plain:
It's not a problem. This can occurs at loci where the methylation of each group are in disjoint ranges- for example all treatment 0 samples have methylation from 0-15, and all treatment 1 samples have methylation between 65-85. This is called "complete separation <http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/mult_pkg/faq/general/complete_separation_logit_models.htm>" and will give p-values of 0, and the warnings you see. The smaller your sample size, the more likely it is to have sites where this happens.

Dhruva

messages.body_plain:
The idea is based on removing principal components that corresponds to a batch effect and reconstructing the data. It is a very crude way of dealing with the problem but it might work, there are other alternatives such as SVA (BioC package)

you have to use first assocComp() to find components associated with your known batches, and then use removeComp() to remove the components associated with batches. see the examples at help pages of those functions.

We are working on dealing with covariates such as known batch effects in other ways. It will hopefully available soon to test as an external script.

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] methylKit input format
messages.body_plain:
You need the additional read counts column to be able to calculate and read the methylation information. If you used sure sureSelect you must have the read counts per CpG or per region somewhere in your pipeline. You should be able to read generic tabular text files with read() function. There are examples of how to read such files in the blog (linked at the methylKit webpage)

best,
Altuna

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the disturbing format, you can assume I understand bed formats and tables in R.

I have some null q values, is that normal ?

We have so much samples that it s hard to send you the files for the tests, I just spot these interval with -48.75 % of methylation and I wanted to check in my initial data what does the single positions look like.
I guess it s not straight forward, my intervall is chr10 from 77155451 to 77155550:

bed :
chr10    77155451    77155550    *    0    0    -48.7489724216988

I can take all the interval positions over 5X in my bismarck output in the controls subjects :
http://nasty.mushroom.free.fr/trucs/control_myCpG.txt

The same for the cases :
http://nasty.mushroom.free.fr/trucs/case_myCpG.txt

Here you have everything ! Except that the filter by coverage is done with 99% and the normalzation is not done, but anyway I can t imagine how we get 48% of differences with those informations.

Thank you for your help !

Le vendredi 14 février 2014 19:22:49 UTC-5, Altuna Akalin a écrit :
> In addition, if you used the same table you sent in bedtools it won't work, it has to be BED format to be used in bedtools.
>
>
> On Sat, Feb 15, 2014 at 1:11 AM, Altuna Akalin <aak...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > the line number shouldn't be there but I guess it comes from the write.table  default argument. In any case, I can not replicate the error with the example data sets. you need to share more information.
> >
> > I need subset of the data and your script that works with that subset that demonstrates the problem. If you can replicate the problem with one of the smaller chromosomes or part of a chromosome that would be good.
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Feb 14, 2014 at 7:46 PM, Raphael Paul Emile <raphael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > The line come from a txt that we did from the object table, what looks weird exactly ?
> > > The head of the file :
> > >
> > > "line" "chr" "start" "end" "strand" "pvalue" "qvalue" "meth.diff"
> > > "1" "1" 10501 10600 "*" 0 0 5.68520504202106
> > > "15" "1" 839351 839450 "*" 8.4821039081362e-14 3.83091276233629e-14 5.85733887513346
> > >
> > > Sup question -> a null p value mean extreeeeeeme significance ?
> > >
> > > We did what you said with bedtool intersect. All the positions in the bed resulting are present in the tile bed resulting for instance ...
> > >
> > >
> > > Le vendredi 14 février 2014 13:05:33 UTC-5, Altuna Akalin a écrit :
> > > > check the region with findOverlaps() fromGRanges, you can coerce methylKit objects to GRanges, and verify if there is really no CpG overlapping. In addition, your object looks weird there might something wrong with the whole object or chromsome names. If you can find a bug or error, send subset of data and script that reproduces the problem.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Feb 14, 2014 at 6:57 PM, <raphael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > We have the same problem checking a region that have a meth.diff around -48% with a q value of 0, with 29 case and 29 controls.
> > > > >
> > > > > "20833" "10" 77155451 77155550 "*" 0 0 -48.7489724216988
> > > > >
> > > > > Now I am looking for positions in this interval and I cannot find any !
> > > > >
> > > > > Le lundi 10 février 2014 18:49:12 UTC-5, Altuna Akalin a écrit :
> > > > > > I wouldn't expect the differentially methylated bases on promoters will be always overlapping with differentially methylated promoters from the regional analysis. One is looking at the bases, the other at regions and when you sum up the methylated and unmethylated bases overlapping with a region you change the statistics, it can go either way, it can push the region to be differentially methylated although individual bases are not DMCs in your thresholds. You see most of your differentially methylated promoters are borderline close to 25% threshold.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The proper way to check and report this it is to find all promoter overlapping DMCs and then check what percent of those promoters overlapping with DMCs are differentially methylated promoters from your promoterMeth.r script. If they never overlap there might be a problem.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > Altuna
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Mon, Feb 10, 2014 at 2:59 PM, Bishwa Ghimire <bishwa....@btk.fi> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > I have (bismark aligned and sorted) 3 control SAMs and 3 treatement SAMs. First, I tried to find differentially methylated bases (attached script diffMeth.r) and later tried to find differentially methylated promoter region  (attached script promoterMeth.r).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In Diff-25p.txt you can see that there are differentially methylated based reported by methylKit. Here, I have included methylated bases only from X chromosome.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In Diff-25p-promoter-tss-features.txt you can see X chromosome promoter region that are differentially methylated.
> > > > > > > But, to my surprise differentially methylated bases (Diff-25p.txt) does not falls in any promoter region interval reported in Diff-25p-promoter-tss-features.txt. For example, in Diff-25p-promoter-tss-features.txt chrX:89409738 - 89409738 promoter region is diffrentially methylated, but there are not any differentially methylated bases within the region if you look at Diff-25p.txt.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Did I do something stupid ?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Regards,
> > > > > > > Bishwa

messages.body_plain:
I figure it out !!!

this weighted.mean=FALSE will save me ! One of my 60 biological replicates with so much coverage on so much positions did drive the difference of methylation in a really strong way.

Thanks a lot for your help and for this tool, I will answer to the method discussion for further stuffs. I guess I will become a strong activist for the update of the tile test with weighted.mean=FALSE !

messages.subject: Creating a myDiff bed file to feed into eDMR
messages.subject_clean: Creating a myDiff bed file to feed into eDMR
messages.body_plain:
My input files are tab delimited text files that look like the following without headers.

chr start end strand coverage %_methylation

I will feed three files into methylKit using the following commands:
#MethylKit Working Script
library(methylKit)

obj=read("NO19_methylKit.txt",sample.id <http://sample.id>="NO19",assembly="hg19",header=TRUE, context="CpG", resolution="base",
          pipeline=list(fraction=TRUE,chr.col=1,start.col=2,end.col=3,
                        strand.col=4, coverage.col=5,freqC.col=6 ),

obj=read("EOC_91_methylKit.txt",sample.id <http://sample.id>="EOC_91",assembly="hg19",header=TRUE, context="CpG", resolution="base",
          pipeline=list(fraction=TRUE,chr.col=1,start.col=2,end.col=3,
                        strand.col=4, coverage.col=5,freqC.col=6 ),

obj=read("EOC_100_3rd_methylKit.txt",sample.id <http://sample.id>="EOC_100",assembly="hg19",header=TRUE, context="CpG", resolution="base",
          pipeline=list(fraction=TRUE,chr.col=1,start.col=2,end.col=3,
                        strand.col=4, coverage.col=5,freqC.col=6 ),
       )

# read the files to a methylRawList object: myobj
myobj=read( file.list,
           sample.id <http://sample.id>=list("NO19","EOC_91","EOC_100"),assembly="hg19",treatment=c(1,0,0))

# get methylation statistics on NO19 in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[1]],plot=F,both.strands=F)

# plot methylation statistics on NO19 in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[1]],plot=T,both.strands=F)

# get methylation statistics on EOC_91 in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[2]],plot=F,both.strands=F)

# plot methylation statistics on EOC_91 in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[2]],plot=T,both.strands=F)

# get methylation statistics on EOC_100 in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[3]],plot=F,both.strands=F)

# plot methylation statistics on EOC_100 in myobj which is a class of methylRawList
getMethylationStats(myobj[[3]],plot=T,both.strands=F)

# see what the data looks like for NO19 in myobj methylRawList
head(myobj[[1]])

# see what the data looks like for EOC_91 in myobj methylRawList
head(myobj[[2]])

# see what the data looks like for EOC_100 in myobj methylRawList
head(myobj[[3]])

# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
# setting destrand=TRUE, will merge reads on both strans of a CpG dinucleotide. This provides better
# coverage, but only advised when looking at CpG methylation
meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE)

# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
#
meth=unite(myobj)

# cluster all samples using correlation distance and return a tree object for plclust
hc = clusterSamples(meth, dist="correlation", method="ward", plot=FALSE)

# plots pair-wise scatter plots from sample set
getCorrelation(meth,plot=TRUE)

# cluster all samples using correlation distance and plot hiarachical clustering
clusterSamples(meth, dist="correlation", method="ward", plot=TRUE)

# plots pair-wise scatter plots from sample set
getCorrelation(meth,plot=TRUE)

# screeplot of principal component analysis.
PCASamples(meth, screeplot=TRUE)

# principal component anlaysis of all samples.
PCASamples(meth)

# calculate differential methylation p-values and q-values
myDiff=calculateDiffMeth(meth)

#########################################################################
At this point I do not know how to create a myDiff bed file with the following format to feed into eDMR

chr start end strand pvalue qvalue meth.diff

##########################################################################

Thanks

Dave

Dear Altuna,

I am trying to use percMethylation() function on my sample data. I am using methylKit0.9.2 version.

percMethylation() seems to give variable results (little variation is expected) depending on how I process my data. I explain the issue with the following options

option1 works with out any error
methylRawList object ==>regionCounts()==>unite()==> percMethylation()

methylRawList object ==>unite()==>regionCounts()==> percMethylation()

 error_percMethylation_function.pdf <https://docs.google.com/file/d/0BxUByyNRRGP9YTB6VFNmTU1iUDA/edit?usp=drive_web>

Kalyan

messages.subject_clean: [methylkit_discussion] Fishers Exact test or Logistics regression test and treatment statement
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Feb 19, 2014 at 7:36 PM, <dklink...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I have two questions that the vignette does not cover very clearly.
>
> If I am comparing 1 control sample to say two or more test samples will the software always force a Logistics regression analysis (I guess using the pool() function will change it to Fishers).
>

pool function will pool the replicates together, and in your case you will have a new data set with one treatment and one control.

> When defining which samples/files are control and treatment does it matter in which order they are loaded or in the read statement or treatment statement.
>
> For example does read have to be treatment first and control second like that below:
>  myobj = read(file.list, sample.id <http://sample.id> = list("treatment1", "treatment2", "control1"),
>
> Then are the treatments always 1 followed by the control being 0.
>  treatment = c(1,1,0),
>

The sample order should match the treatment vector order, meaning that files that are treatment should have 1s and the files that are control should have 0s in corresponding locations of the treatment vector. That's the most important thing. The internal code in calculateDiffMeth() subsets the methylBase object based on the treatment vector to create a treatment and control group.

messages.body_plain:
Dear dave,

In case you are asking about saving a R object of GRanges class (In this case myDMR2 as explained by Sheng) into a text file you can do the following:

Option 1:
# You should have installed rtracklayer library
# This option will write a bed formatted file of the dmrs
# Remember that this option doesnt write any of the metadata
# Check the help for exact command usage for export.bed

library(rtracklayer)
>export.bed(myDMR2,"my_dmr2.bed")

Option2:
# Simply write the GRanges object/myDMR2 into a text file
# Check help for exact command usage
#This option writes every column into the text file separated by single space

> my_dmr2=as.data.frame(myDMR2)
>write.table(my_dmr2, file="my_dmr2.txt", quote=F, row.names=F)

Regards,
Kalyan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

Try this?

getGR=function(myDMR, subject){
  ind=findOverlaps(subject,myDMR)
  subject[unique(ind@queryHits)]
}

# genebody promoters
gr=getGR(myDMR, genebody$promoter)
gr2=as.data.frame(gr)
write.table(gr2, file="gr2.txt", quote=F, row.names=F, col.names=F)

# CpG island:
CpGi.gr=getGR(myDMR, cpgi$cpgis)
CpGi.gr2=as.data.frame(CpGi.gr)
write.table(gr2, file="CpGigr2.txt", quote=F, row.names=F, col.names=F)

Cheers,
Sheng

messages.body_plain:
Altuna has pointed a very important issue in the analysis of methylation data. I would like to add one more point and I welcome further comments on this.

Performing 'regionscounts' on a methylRawList object may include the CpGs that are not covered in all the samples. From my point of view, this also leads to bias in calculation of the methylation status. To, expand this point consider this case. A 'promoter' of length 1.2kb may have 40 CpGs covered in sample1 (spread uniformly across the length) and sample2 with just 20 CpGs covered (on side of the promoter and not on other side). If we perform 'regioncounts' at this stage, we tend to calculate the methylation status from 40 CpGs of sample1 and just 20CpGs of sample2 which is biased due to under representation in sample2.

One possible way is to perform 'unite' function first and perform 'regioncounts' on the methylBase obj. This ensures that we consider only the common 20 CpGs in both samples. Some may find this option as conservative and wastage of methylation information in the data. But, my understanding is that in such a case we are more close to accuracy and comparison happens between CpGs of similar/dissimilar status at the same location. Additional CpGs (20 CpGs from Sample1) do add additional information and tweaks/neutralizes the methylations status of the region in their favour which are not represented in Sample2.

Regards,
Kalyan

On 24 February 2014 22:05, Altuna Akalin <aak...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I suggest take one of differentially methylated windows, find Cs overlapping with it, and do the differential methylation calculation per base for those regions. Check the percent methylation differences for those Cs, are they close to your cutoff ? Also see below
>
>  I don't expect one to one correspondence between DMRs and DMCs. DMR calculation doesn't really depend on individual bases being differentially methylated, the number of methylated Cs and unmethylated Cs pooled over a region, that sort of pooling can cause differences in correspondence, where a DMR may not have DMCs. But main reason could be the following: in your DMRs there might be bases that are not covered in all samples, pooling counts per region will ignore whether or not each base covered in all samples or not. This is practical for sparsely covered genomes, because doing per base analysis will remove the bases from the analysis if they are not covered in all samples. By doing regional analysis you keep the information from the bases that are not covered in all samples.

I agree with you. If you look at my original post you will find that after reading my files and filtering by coverage I united my samples. Just then I calculated DiffMeth. I think that the example that you bring is a highly likely  scenario (also highly dependent of coverage). Besides your suggestion I also think that using smaller tiles and shorter steps can avoid these kind of problems. For mouse and human and outside of CpG island you have one CpG every 110 bp (in average). may be a 250 bp tile will be more conservative than a 1000 bp one. In a future it will  be also nice if the package can tile and step in function of the CpG density.

Alejandro

El martes, 25 de febrero de 2014 02:39:44 UTC-5, Kalyan Kumar Pasumarthy escribió:

> Altuna has pointed a very important issue in the analysis of methylation data. I would like to add one more point and I welcome further comments on this.
>
> Performing 'regionscounts' on a methylRawList object may include the CpGs that are not covered in all the samples. From my point of view, this also leads to bias in calculation of the methylation status. To, expand this point consider this case. A 'promoter' of length 1.2kb may have 40 CpGs covered in sample1 (spread uniformly across the length) and sample2 with just 20 CpGs covered (on side of the promoter and not on other side). If we perform 'regioncounts' at this stage, we tend to calculate the methylation status from 40 CpGs of sample1 and just 20CpGs of sample2 which is biased due to under representation in sample2.
>
> One possible way is to perform 'unite' function first and perform 'regioncounts' on the methylBase obj. This ensures that we consider only the common 20 CpGs in both samples. Some may find this option as conservative and wastage of methylation information in the data. But, my understanding is that in such a case we are more close to accuracy and comparison happens between CpGs of similar/dissimilar status at the same location. Additional CpGs (20 CpGs from Sample1) do add additional information and tweaks/neutralizes the methylations status of the region in their favour which are not represented in Sample2.
>

>
> Regards,
> Kalyan
>
>

> On 24 February 2014 22:05, Altuna Akalin <aak...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I suggest take one of differentially methylated windows, find Cs overlapping with it, and do the differential methylation calculation per base for those regions. Check the percent methylation differences for those Cs, are they close to your cutoff ? Also see below
> >
> >  I don't expect one to one correspondence between DMRs and DMCs. DMR calculation doesn't really depend on individual bases being differentially methylated, the number of methylated Cs and unmethylated Cs pooled over a region, that sort of pooling can cause differences in correspondence, where a DMR may not have DMCs. But main reason could be the following: in your DMRs there might be bases that are not covered in all samples, pooling counts per region will ignore whether or not each base covered in all samples or not. This is practical for sparsely covered genomes, because doing per base analysis will remove the bases from the analysis if they are not covered in all samples. By doing regional analysis you keep the information from the bases that are not covered in all samples.
> >
> > Best,
> > Altuna
> >
> >

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] annotation file in gff3 format
messages.body_plain:
Yes, as Kalyan pointed out read.bed would work if you are only interested in TSS and stop codon. You either read a file that contains those, or you can try to get those out of the GFF after reading in.

read.bed removes the chromosome names that have "_" by default, you can set it not to do that by setting up the second argument to FALSE.

Best,
Altuna

> I was expecting that if one tile shows up as significantly differentially methylated, at least one cytosine must be differentially methylated.   But if I understand correctly you said that even though not single C in a tile is differentially methylated, the contribution of many not significant differences can produce a consolidated differentially methylated tile. I feel it kind of contra-intuitive but if possible do you think that my more that 1000 DMR found in chr1 showed up in this way?

This kind of effect could occur when pooling, DMRs and DMCs should not differ drastically if that is the sole reason. That's why I asked if the DMRs have borderline DMCs? I don't think 1000 DMRs can show up this way but it would be good to check if there are borderline DMCs in them. I also suggest that you don't use overlapping windows, this might  inflate the overall number of DMRs and not good for multiple testing correction. The correction assumes the tests are independent, if windows are overlapping tests are not independent.

> Then you said that other reason could be lack of coverage. If I understand correctly you are saying that most of my DMR come out of regions that were poorly covered (and the many often one of the samples has not reads) or "bias ly" covered...may be 30 or 50 reads in 3 of the four libraries but one got zero.

I think this is more probable reason where you have non-uniform coverage over the bases. But if your tiles are small, you can get away with this. Literature suggest that CpGs (not sure this is true for all species I remember a publication about bees and we did something similar for human) close-by are correlated in their methylation levels. So if you take that into account, tilling on small windows could work and can interpolate methylation levels of regions even you don't have coverage over the bases.

>
> Are both explanation indicating that is not god idea to perform calculateDiffMeth in a tiled genome?
> Instead of filter by coverage in all, is there any way of filter by average??

I think tiling could work. You can try to show first spatial correlation between CpGs or Cs, if there is than you can tile and then unite(). If not, the only option is to first create a methylBase object containing bases then tile. This will remove bases that are not covered in all samples then you will be able to tile just using those bases

messages.body_plain:
>
> Following the discussion and advise provided by Altuna I found out that most of my DMR are called in regions of the genome with very low coverage ( less than 5 reads per cytosine). However I think that I have a decent coverage.
>

In my opinion, you should remove everything below 10X before you do any analysis.

> At first I would like to find differentially methylated cytosines (since  I'm doing methyl seq to have single base resolution).
>
> ###After reading my files I create an "myobj" containing them.
> ### I first filtered by a coverage.
>
> > filtered.myobj=filterByCoverage(myobj,lo.count=8,lo.perc=NULL,hi.count=NULL,hi.perc=99.9)
>
> #### Then I will merge samples , but HERE I HAVE A QUESTION
>
> ### IT IS THIS?
>
> > meth=unite(myobj, destrand = FALSE)
>
> #### or rather is this?
>
> > meth=unite (filtered.myobj, destrand = FALSE)
>

the second option is what you want to do here, I think: meth=unite (filtered.myobj, destrand = FALSE)

>
> #### also here I have another doubt. I will like to use destrand = TRUE, when focusing in CG methylation. But what happens is that after filtering information for many CG remain in only one strand.

CG methylation is mostly symmetric (in many human samples I looked at). If that's the case for your species, it doesn't matter if filtering removes coverage on one strand mostly. You can still treat them equally and pool them.

> #### CAN I FIRST CREATE A methylBase object and then filter element of this object in term of coverage?

Yes you can do this, but not with the  filterByCoverage() function but using the [] notation.
You should be able to subset methylBase object the way you would subset the rows of a data.frame.

assume "mbase" is a methylBase object. The code below will create a new methylBase object where
the coverage values from the 1st and 2nd sample above 10.

mbase[mbase$coverage1>10 & mbase$coverage2>10, ]

Best,
Altuna
